text:
According to the Environmental Statement drafted by the Bureau of Sport Fisheries and Wildlife, Federal management control is desirable because some States do not have regulatory control of species that appear on the list and the Secretary cannot prohibit interstate shipment. Adoption of the Model Nongame Wildlife law by all States would accomplish this objective and provide the States, who possess the only adequate enforcement machinery, authority to act.
History shows that legislation like the Endangered Species Conservation Act is not effective, overall, in enhancing, maintaining or even protecting wildlife species. The Migratory Bird Treaty Act of 1918, as amended, gives the Secretary of Interior authority to regulate the taking and transporting of certain migratory birds. Yet, over 65 percent of the birds listed in the 1968 edition of Rare and Endangered Species were included in the 1918 Act. In 1940, the Eagle Act was passed to protect all subspecies of the Bald Eagle. However, the Southern Bald Eagle is listed as endangered and, according to the Bureau of Sport Fisheries and Wildlife, is still decreasing in number.
Of species within the continental United States appearing on the lists, 80 percent of the mammals and nearly 100 percent of the birds have habitat alteration by man listed as one of the primary causes of population decline. It would have made little difference if these species were under Federal jurisdiction or State jurisdiction; population reductions would still have occurred. Land clearing, pesticides, development, and merely the presence of humans have all been responsible.
Purchasing land and creating wildlife refuges may help local populations, but the overall trend will continue downward if land-use practices do not change. This should be the target for Federal legislation, not whether management control is in Federal or State hands.
